segments.say: Ask a nurse, a police officer or a teacher, and many will tell you the same thing. Something odd happens on the night of the full moon. The emergency room fills up. The calls come in. The children are wild, and the whole shift seems to run a little off its course. The belief is ancient, and it's built right into our language. The word lunatic comes from luna, the Latin for moon.

For centuries, people in many cultures have linked the moon to madness, sleeplessness and strange behaviour. Ancient writers, including Aristotle and Pliny, recorded the idea that the moon influenced the brain, which they thought was the wettest organ of the body and so subject to the tides. It was a neat piece of reasoning, even if the premise was wrong.

The belief is still common today. Surveys of nurses, doctors and teachers have found that large numbers believe the full moon affects behaviour, and some studies in the 1980s and 1990s found that around half to eighty percent of health workers agreed. It's not a belief that only the uneducated hold. It's one that people who work with the public hold from experience.

James Rotton and Ivan Kelly gathered thirty-seven studies that looked for a link between the phases of the moon and things like crime, psychiatric admissions, suicides, births and accidents. They combined them into a single analysis. The moon, they concluded, was not related to any of those things in a reliable way.

show.what: Much ado about the full moon: a meta-analysis of lunar-lunacy research

segments.say: In their words, the moon had no significant effect on behaviour that could be proved. The few studies that appeared to find something were small, and did not agree with each other on what the effect was. It's the pattern you would expect from chance. Later reviews, including one by Kelly, Rotton and Culver in 1996, came to the same conclusion.

show.title: Studies analysed
show.label: looking for links between the moon and human behaviour

segments.say: It's a long list, and across it, the result is the same. The full moon doesn't reliably change any of them. That doesn't mean that individual busy nights don't occur, of course. It means that they're no more likely on a full moon than any other night.

If the evidence is so clear, why do so many experienced people believe it? The answer is a familiar one. It's all about which nights we remember. When a full moon coincides with a chaotic shift, we think, there it is, I knew it. When the full moon passes quietly, we don't think anything at all.

Psychologists call this an illusory correlation. When two unusual things happen together, such as a bright moon and a busy night, they stick in the memory. When they don't happen together, there's nothing to notice. Over the years, we build up a stock of memorable coincidences, and it feels like a pattern.

Loren and Jean Chapman, working at the University of Wisconsin in the 1960s, showed how readily people see correlations that aren't there. They found that people, including trained professionals, would report a relationship between two things when they were expected to go together, even when the data showed no such thing. The expectation created the pattern.

show.what: Genesis of popular but erroneous psychodiagnostic observations

segments.say: Think of all the full moons that came and went without incident. Most of them went unnoticed, because nothing happened. And what about all the chaotic nights that came on days with no moon at all? We blame the weather, the day of the week, or the time of the month. The full moon gets credit when it's there and no blame when it's not.

show.cap: The case of the quiet moon

segments.say: Notice that the moon is a very convenient explanation. It's something that everyone can see, and it comes round regularly, so there's always a candidate. Real causes of busy nights are often more complicated, and not nearly as easy to point to.

show.title: Why the moon takes the blame
items: It has a long cultural reputation

segments.say: But here's where the story becomes more interesting. In 2013, a Swiss team led by Christian Cajochen at the University of Basel reported something about the moon that got a lot of attention. They had re-analysed data from an earlier sleep study, and they found that people slept a little worse around the full moon.

The researchers looked back at the records of thirty-three volunteers who had slept in a laboratory, with no windows, for several nights. Around the full moon, they found, deep sleep was reduced by about thirty percent, people took about five minutes longer to fall asleep, and they slept for about twenty minutes less. It sounded like a real effect.

show.what: Evidence that the lunar cycle influences human sleep

segments.say: There was a catch. The original study had not been designed to look at the moon at all. The researchers went back to the data afterwards, and looked for a pattern. That's a risky way to work, because if you hunt through enough data, you'll nearly always find something. The result needed to be tested with a study built for that purpose.

A year later, a team led by Michael Cordi at the University of Basel and the University of Fribourg looked at a much bigger set of sleep records. They examined more than twelve hundred participants, over more than two thousand nights, and found no reliable link between the moon and sleep. The effect seen in the smaller study didn't hold up.

show.what: Lunar cycle effects on sleep and the file drawer problem

segments.say: It's a nice illustration of how science works. A small, surprising result is reported. Others try to repeat it with more data. And, if it fails, the field quietly updates. The moon may still affect some individuals, but a strong and reliable effect on sleep is not supported.

show.title: Sleep records in the larger analysis
show.label: volunteers, with no reliable lunar effect on sleep

segments.say: So where does this leave us? The evidence for effects of the moon on crime, madness and accidents is very weak. The evidence for sleep is mixed and not convincing. A fair position is to stay open to new data, but to doubt that the moon has the dramatic influence that folklore gives it.

It's also worth remembering that a bright moon in a bedroom window can keep someone awake, and that people who believe that they'll sleep badly on a full moon may well do so. Expectation, again, may be doing some of the work.

show.title: A fair summary
items: No reliable effect on crime or admissions
No reliable effect on births or suicides
Strong beliefs because the coincidences stand out

segments.say: It's a beautiful sight, and it deserves to be enjoyed for what it is. A bright light in the sky, looking over a world that, by every measure we can make, is behaving much as it does on any other night.

show.cap: A full moon over quiet rooftops

segments.say: There's a pleasing kindness in letting the moon off the hook. A hard night at work is a hard night at work, and a restless child is a restless child. Looking for the real reason, like tiredness, hunger, stress or an overfull day, usually gives you something that you can actually do something about.

So what did we learn? That thirty-seven studies found no reliable link between the moon and behaviour. That illusory correlation makes coincidences feel like patterns. That a surprising sleep result didn't hold up in a larger study. And that the most useful response to a strong belief is to test it, politely.

Another popular belief is that more babies are born at the full moon. Hospital staff often swear to it. But studies of hundreds of thousands of births have found no such pattern. One large study of more than half a million births in the United States over several years found no link between the phase of the moon and the number of births. The memorable busy night, again, was the one that was remembered.

If you wanted to test the full moon belief yourself, how would you do it? You'd need to count all the nights, not just the busy ones, and compare full moon nights with others. You'd need to decide in advance what counts as strange behaviour. And you'd need someone who didn't know the moon's phase to do the counting. That is, in essence, what the researchers did, and it's what separates a hunch from a finding.

There's a human reason why the moon belief lasts. A difficult night at work is frustrating, and a reason, any reason, makes it more bearable. It's easier to say that it's the full moon than that no one quite knows why everything is going wrong. The moon is a harmless scapegoat, and it gives a stressful shift a story and a shape, which may be why people find it hard to give up.

In the next story, we'll look at a skill that many of us are proud of, or at least rely upon. Doing two things at once. It's in job adverts, in daily life and on every phone, and the research on it is unusually blunt.
